Subject: Model fit & tool-calling evals for FinLytics — Post-call recap and next steps

Hi Elena —

Thanks again for taking the call today. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we stay aligned: 

- Goals we scoped: reliably extract structured transactions from monthly statements and enrich with merchant categorization. Critical requirements: JSON-schema-compliant output, deterministic field types, and robust retries for transient mis-parses.
- Recommended model candidates (tradeoffs):
  - redwood-optimized-llama-70b-q4 (best quality on complex long-context parsing; higher cost, higher memory)
  - open-llama-13b-4bit (good latency/cost balance for <1s generation on short docs)
  - redwood-instruct-3b (fast and cheap for simple extraction, lower pass-rate on nested structures)

What I attached: finlytics_prompt_set_v1.json (prompt examples / expected schema) and a short benchmark summary link. Our usual approach for tool/function-calling and structured output evals is: run your sample through the two recommended model configs, validate JSON schema compliance (we run schema fuzzing + validators), compute a pass-rate, and surface regression / hallucination examples. For retries we test 0/1/2 retry policies with exponential backoff and idempotency tokens to measure improvements vs cost.

Next steps I propose:
1) You share a small anonymized sample (5-10 docs) and the success criteria (e.g., 95% schema pass, max 2% hallucination) — attach as CSV if possible.
2) We run a focused eval (3 models x retry policies) and share a short report with recommended model + config.
3) If results look good, we scope a pilot (throughput targets, SLA) and pricing.

Can you confirm data share and whether procurement needs an NDA/DSA first? I cc'd Aditya and Neha to help scope the eval and run the schema checks.

Cheers,
Marissa Cole

Thanks Elena — appreciate the quick turnaround.

We pulled a short internal benchmark summary against similar extraction workloads (attached as model_benchmark_summary_20260602.pdf). High-level: redwood-optimized-llama-70b-q4 shows ~96% schema pass on nested transaction extraction at a median latency of ~380ms (single doc, p95 ~520ms) on Dedicated capacity; open-llama-13b-4bit shows ~88% pass at median ~220ms (p95 ~420ms). The tradeoff is clear: higher pass-rate vs cost and memory.

On your questions about retries and idempotency: our runtime supports idempotency tokens and a configurable retry/backoff policy. For structured outputs we evaluate two modes:
- function-calling mode (structured JSON returned by the model) + schema validation on the output; failures trigger optional retry with modified system prompt that emphasizes schema constraints.
- post-processing validators: run a strict JSON schema validator and, for non-compliant outputs, attempt heuristic correction + 1 retry.

We'll run an official focused eval if you share the sample. Proposed evaluation acceptance criteria (we can tweak):
- Schema pass-rate >= 94% for primary model OR improvement >6% vs baseline model.
- Hallucination rate <= 2% (external IDs or invented merchants).
- Stable retries: one retry should raise pass-rate by at least 4 percentage points on average.

Attached: eval_results_tool_calling_v1.xlsx (template with metrics we report). If this looks good, we'll schedule the run — estimated turnaround 3 business days after sample + access.

Also linking the HubSpot deal and a DocuSign template if procurement prefers that route.

Best,
Marissa

Hi all —

A couple of technical notes on how we'll validate structured outputs and retries so expectations are clear: 

1) Validators: we run JSON Schema draft-07 validators plus a lightweight schema-fuzzing pass (randomized field ordering, extra fields). We record both strict-pass (exact match to schema) and tolerant-pass (correct types and required fields present).

2) Retry policy: default is up to 2 retries with exponential backoff (200ms -> 600ms). Each retry uses an augmented system prompt that includes the previous model output and an explicit "Return only valid JSON matching this schema" instruction and an idempotency token to prevent double-processing of downstream tools.

3) Metrics we capture: strict pass-rate, tolerant pass-rate, average latency including retries, tokens per document, and per-field error rates (missing/incorrect types).

4) For deterministic post-processing we support an optional function-caller that maps model JSON to a typed proto and runs a deterministic sanitizer. This can be used as a final gate before ingestion.

If FinLytics wants, we can run the eval on Redwood Dedicated to get stable latency profiles — I'll include a rough cost estimate in the report (link above).

Happy to sync on a short tech call if needed.

— Aditya
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
